title: Everyone has a vocation
hookLine: vocation means calling, and every baptized person has one

lines: HERE I AM, YOU CALLED ME.
SPEAK, LORD, FOR THY SERVANT HEARETH.
cards: It's night in the house of God at Shiloh. A boy named Samuel is asleep near the ark. A voice says his name.
He runs to the old priest, Eli: here I am, you called me. Eli says he didn't; go back to bed. It happens again.
Then the text says the Lord called Samuel again the third time, and this time Eli understands. If it comes again, he tells the boy, answer. It comes.
And Samuel says, in the Douay-Rheims: "Speak, Lord, for thy servant heareth." A whole life starts with a name said in the dark. Today, a new stretch on callings.

teach.b: Back on day six hundred sixty-seven, Good Shepherd Sunday, you met the Church's day of prayer for vocations. A vocation is a calling: not first a job or a career, but a voice, and somebody answering it.
Praying for vocations can sound like praying only for priests, sisters and brothers. That's a real calling, and this stretch will get to it. But the Church's teaching starts wider.
The Second Vatican Council said that all the faithful, whatever their state of life, are called to the fullness of Christian life and the perfection of love.

teach.h: ONE CALL TO HOLINESS FOR ALL.
teach.b: The Catechism repeats it: the call to holiness is for everyone.

It goes back to a hard sentence of Jesus in the Sermon on the Mount, in the Douay-Rheims: "Be you therefore perfect, as also your heavenly Father is perfect." Not said to monks: Matthew says the crowds heard it.
So the Catholic picture has two layers. The first call comes to every baptized person, the same for all: to holiness, to love.

teach.h: THEN A SHAPE FOR EACH LIFE.
teach.b: Then each life answers it in a particular shape: marriage, the single life, religious vows, holy orders.

teach.h: WALK WORTHY OF THE VOCATION IN WHICH YOU ARE CALLED.
teach.b: Paul, writing from prison to a whole church of ordinary people, puts the first layer plainly: "I therefore, a prisoner in the Lord, beseech you that you walk worthy of the vocation in which you are called."
So the nurse on a night shift, the dad at school pickup, the student cramming: none of them is waiting for a calling to arrive someday.
Catholic teaching says they already have one, and they're living it, or not, right now.

how: Catholics speak of a universal call to holiness that every baptized person shares, and of particular vocations: marriage, the single life, religious life and holy orders. Parishes pray for vocations, and people discerning a calling often talk it through with a priest, sister or spiritual director.

games.q: you're Eli, an old priest. the boy Samuel has woken you for the third time, sure you called him. you didn't. what do you tell him?
o: stop dreaming and go to sleep.
go lie down, and if it comes again, answer the Lord.
come sleep in my room so it stops.
games.why: Eli understands it's the Lord calling. he sends Samuel back to listen, and Samuel answers, "speak, Lord, for thy servant heareth."

practice: Not the next five years: who is in front of you this season, needing something only you can give? Let one face, or one task, come up and stay with it.
If you pray, borrow Samuel's words, speak, Lord, for thy servant heareth; if you don't, let the question sit, unanswered for now.

wordCard.voice: Vocation. A calling. In Catholic teaching, every baptized person's call to holiness, lived out in a particular state of life. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: called. The first call is the same for everyone: holiness, love. See you tomorrow.
